title: Pre-IPO Investing: How Access Works, Where Returns Come From, and What Can Go Wrong
summary: Your edge through the companies, trends, and AI-driven tools shaping the future of private wealth, powered by Goodfin.
body_text: TL;DR: Pre-IPO investing means acquiring equity in a private company before it lists on a public exchange. The structural case is real — but access is gated, liquidity is constrained, and exits rarely arrive on the timeline investors expect. This piece orients you to the asset class. Linked chapters go deeper on each component. The IPO Is Not the Beginning For most investors, a company's public debut is when it enters the picture. That's also, increasingly, when the fastest growth is behind it. Between 1980 and 2024, the median age of companies going public more than doubled — from roughly 8 years in the mid-1990s to 14 years in 2024, according to Jay Ritter's long-running IPO dataset at the University of Florida. Median revenue at IPO, inflation-adjusted, rose from $64 million to $218 million over the same period. Companies reach public markets later, larger, and more valued than they once did. The implication is straightforward: more of a company's highest-growth phase now occurs while it is still private. By the time shares trade on a public exchange, a significant portion of the compounding has already happened. Pre-IPO investing is the attempt to participate before that window closes — with real constraints that this piece will lay out. What "Pre-IPO" Actually Means The term gets used loosely. In practice, it refers to equity in a private company, acquired through one of several distinct structures. Which one you're in matters — for your legal rights, your liquidity options, your tax treatment, and your claim on proceeds if an exit occurs. Primary shares are newly issued shares sold by the company in a funding round. The company receives the capital; investors receive equity. Access typically flows to institutional investors — VC and growth equity funds — though platforms now aggregate individual capital into these rounds. Aggregation is not the same as access. Pooled capital can enter a round at the same headline valuation as institutional investors, or it can enter through a structure that layers in additional fees, weaker rights, and no direct position on the cap table. The difference is in how the deal is sourced, structured, and priced — not just whether participation was possible. Secondary shares are existing shares sold by a current holder: an employee, an early angel, a fund seeking liquidity. No capital goes to the company. Secondary transactions involve their own mechanics — transfer restrictions, company consent rights, pricing relative to the last round — that warrant separate treatment. Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) are the most common structure through which individual accredited investors access private companies. An SPV is a legal entity — typically an LLC — created to pool capital from multiple investors into a single investment. You hold an interest in the SPV; the SPV holds shares in the company. The SPV manager handles legal documentation, company communications, and investor reporting. VC and growth equity funds provide indirect exposure across a portfolio of private companies. A single manager makes all allocation decisions; you gain diversification but relinquish selection control, with capital locked up for the fund's duration. Who Can Invest — and Why the Gate Exists Pre-IPO investments in the United States are restricted to accredited investors under SEC rules . The thresholds for individuals: Net worth exceeding $1 million , excluding your primary residence Annual income exceeding $200,000 individually, or $300,000 jointly, for the past two years Holders of Series 7, Series 65, or Series 82 licenses, regardless of wealth The threshold exists because private securities are exempt from the disclosure requirements that apply to public companies. Public companies file financials, risk factors, and quarterly reports. Private companies owe no equivalent transparency to outside investors. The accredited investor standard is a regulatory proxy — imperfect, and increasingly debated — for investors capable of evaluating that opacity. As of 2024, roughly 18% of U.S. households qualify. The number has risen steadily as the nominal thresholds, set in 1982, have not been adjusted for inflation. Legal eligibility is necessary but not sufficient. Historically, even accredited investors lacked access to high-demand opportunities without existing institutional relationships or the ability to write large checks. That gap — practical, not legal — is what platforms in this space are built to close. Not all of them close it the same way. The distinction that matters is between access as availability and access as curation: whether the deals on offer have been evaluated for quality, positioned to protect the individual investor, and priced to reflect actual risk — not just made available because someone agreed to list them. Where Returns May Come From The return case for pre-IPO investing rests on a few structural arguments. They are worth distinguishing, because they carry different risks and apply differently to any given deal. Growth capture. Companies going public later means more appreciation is occurring privately. An investor who enters at a lower valuation — before the growth is fully priced in — can potentially capture a portion of what a public market investor would miss entirely. Illiquidity premium. You cannot easily sell a private investment. Markets rationally price that constraint into expected returns — illiquid investments must offer more to attract capital. Whether any specific deal prices the illiquidity fairly is a judgment that depends heavily on entry valuation. Access scarcity. The most sought-after companies are oversubscribed. Investors who can participate capture value that others simply cannot reach. This premium is real, but fragile — it depends on whether the access is to genuinely high-quality opportunities, and at what terms. Terms go beyond price : the legal structure of your position, your place on the cap table, and whether the deal was sourced because it was desirable or because it was available. Secondary discounts. Shares in secondary transactions are sometimes available below the company's last primary round valuation. That gap can represent a margin of safety. It can also reflect what the seller knows. A discount is not automatically a bargain. Whether these arguments apply to a specific investment depends on what you're paying, what you're buying, and what happens to the company. How Liquidity Actually Behaves This is where most investors are surprised. The path from investment to realized return is narrower and less predictable than it looks. The mechanics are worth being direct about. Transfer restrictions. Even when a willing buyer exists, you may not be able to sell. Most private companies hold a right of first refusal (ROFR): before you transfer shares to a third party, the company can match the offer and buy them instead. Others require board approval for any secondary transfer. These provisions can block or significantly delay a sale regardless of market conditions. Post-IPO lock-ups. When a company does go public, pre-IPO investors typically face a lock-up period — usually 90 to 180 days — during which they cannot sell. This is when insider selling pressure is highest and volatility most pronounced. The price on listing day is not the price at which you exit. Tender offers. Company-sponsored or third-party tender offers have become an important liquidity channel as IPO timelines lengthen. Nasdaq Private Market facilitated approximately $15 billion in tender offers in 2025 . Participation is not guaranteed and is often capped. The exit may not arrive. Several high-profile companies pushed IPO timelines by 12 to 18 months in 2025 due to market conditions. Others have stayed private indefinitely, raised down rounds, or failed. An absence of public market pricing does not signal stability — it signals that the instability is less visible. Plan for a minimum hold of 3 to 7 years . In many cases, longer. Key Risks Valuation opacity. Private valuations are set by negotiation at a point in time, not by continuous market pricing. A valuation from a peak-cycle funding round offers no protection if the company's next event — an IPO, a new raise, an acquisition — prices it lower. Information asymmetry. Private companies are not required to disclose what public companies must. You are evaluating an investment with less information than the lead investors who set the price. In secondary transactions especially, sellers often have reasons for wanting liquidity that are not visible to buyers. Dilution. Future funding rounds create new shares, reducing your percentage ownership. Anti-dilution provisions and pro-rata rights exist, but they are more commonly available to institutional lead investors than to individuals investing through SPVs. Fee drag. SPV managers charge management fees and carried interest — typically around 20% of profits. These reduce net returns materially over a multi-year hold. Model the full fee structure before committing. Concentration. A single pre-IPO position is an undiversified bet. Return distributions in private markets are far wider than in public ones — the gap between a strong outcome and a complete loss is larger. Diversification matters more here, not less. Liquidity need. If circumstances change — a home purchase, a business need, an emergency — a private market investment cannot be liquidated on demand. Invest only what you can genuinely leave untouched. Portfolio Fit Most allocation frameworks for HNW investors suggest keeping alternatives — private equity, venture, pre-IPO — between 10% and 30% of investable assets, scaled to liquidity needs and time horizon. For investors entering private markets for the first time, diversifying across multiple companies at manageable check sizes is more defensible than concentrating in a single name. When check sizes fall, the question shifts from whether to invest in private markets to how to build across them — across companies, stages, and sectors rather than resting on a single outcome. That is a different kind of investor behavior, and it produces a different kind of portfolio. Before You Invest: A Decision Checklist Structure. Am I buying primary shares, secondary shares, or an SPV interest? Do I understand what I actually own? Liquidity horizon. Can I leave this capital untouched for 5 to 7+ years? Valuation reference. What was the last primary round valuation? What am I paying relative to it? Fees. What are the management fee and carry? What do they mean for net returns across exit scenarios? Transfer restrictions. Could ROFR or board approval requirements prevent a sale before a formal exit? Dilution protection. Do I have pro-rata rights or anti-dilution provisions? Exit scenarios. What are the realistic paths to liquidity — IPO, acquisition, tender offer, secondary sale — and what does each return at current valuation? Portfolio sizing. What percentage of my investable assets does this represent? Information quality. What do I actually know about this company, and what am I taking on trust? For educational purposes only. Not investment advice. Investing in private markets carries significant risk, including possible loss of principal. Past performance does not indicate future results. Goodfin is a technology platform, not a registered investment adviser.

title: Grupo 2 NIIF: quiénes aplican y cómo implementar
summary: Si tu empresa en Colombia no cotiza en bolsa, no es una entidad de interés público y tampoco es una microempresa, lo más probable es que pertenezca al Grupo 2 de NIIF, el grupo intermedio que aplica la NIIF para las Pymes. Sin embargo, la clasificación no siempre es obvia: muchas compañías creen que están en el grupo equivocado porque solo miran uno de los tres criterios (activos, empleados o ingresos), cuando la norma exige mirarlos en conjunto y con reglas de prioridad específicas.
body_text: Si tu empresa en Colombia no cotiza en bolsa, no es una entidad de interés público y tampoco es una microempresa, lo más probable es que pertenezca al Grupo 2 de NIIF , el grupo intermedio que aplica la NIIF para las Pymes. Sin embargo, la clasificación no siempre es obvia: muchas compañías creen que están en el grupo equivocado porque solo miran uno de los tres criterios (activos, empleados o ingresos), cuando la norma exige mirarlos en conjunto y con reglas de prioridad específicas. Este artículo reúne en un solo lugar lo que la mayoría de guías deja disperso: los criterios exactos de clasificación, las diferencias frente al Grupo 1 y al Grupo 3, la regla de permanencia de tres años, el paso a paso real de implementación y los errores más frecuentes que cometen las pymes colombianas al hacer la transición. ¿Qué es el Grupo 2 de NIIF? El Grupo 2 es uno de los tres grupos en los que la Ley 1314 de 2009 clasificó a los preparadores de información financiera en Colombia para efectos de la convergencia hacia estándares internacionales. Las entidades de este grupo deben aplicar la NIIF para las Pymes , un estándar simplificado frente a las NIIF Plenas (Grupo 1), pero más exigente que la contabilidad simplificada del Grupo 3 (microempresas). El marco técnico normativo del Grupo 2 está compilado en el Decreto 2420 de 2015 (Decreto Único Reglamentario de las Normas de Contabilidad, de Información Financiera y de Aseguramiento de la Información), específicamente en su Anexo 2, y ha sido actualizado por decretos posteriores como el 2483 de 2018, el 1670 de 2021 y enmiendas más recientes que ajustan secciones puntuales del estándar. Las entidades del Grupo 2 deben aplicar este marco a sus estados financieros individuales, separados, consolidados y combinados , según corresponda a su estructura societaria. ¿Quiénes conforman el Grupo 2? Criterios de clasificación De acuerdo con el artículo 1.1.2.1 del Decreto 2420 de 2015, pertenecen al Grupo 2 las entidades que: No cumplen los requisitos para estar en el Grupo 1 (NIIF Plenas). No son emisoras de valores ni entidades de interés público. Cumplen alguno de estos parámetros de tamaño: Criterio Umbral para Grupo 2 Activos totales Entre 500 y 30.000 SMMLV Planta de personal Entre 11 y 200 trabajadores Microempresa con ingresos altos Activos hasta 500 SMMLV o máximo 10 trabajadores, pero con ingresos brutos anuales iguales o superiores a 6.000 SMMLV Combinación de parámetros distintos Cuando activos y empleados no coinciden en el mismo rango, prevalece el criterio de activos totales Puntos que casi ningún artículo aclara bien: Una empresa no pasa automáticamente al Grupo 1 solo por superar los 200 empleados o los 30.000 SMMLV en activos. Para quedar en Grupo 1 sin ser emisora de valores ni entidad de interés público, además debe cumplir al menos uno de estos criterios adicionales: ser subordinada o sucursal de una compañía extranjera que aplique NIIF Plenas, ser subordinada o matriz de una compañía nacional que deba aplicarlas, ser matriz, asociada o negocio conjunto de entidades extranjeras que apliquen NIIF Plenas, o realizar importaciones/exportaciones que superen el 50% de sus compras o ventas. Si solo supera el umbral de tamaño pero no cumple ninguno de esos criterios adicionales, permanece en el Grupo 2 . El Grupo 2 funciona, en la práctica, como el grupo residual : quedan en él las entidades que no califican para el Grupo 1 ni para el Grupo 3. Una empresa del Grupo 3 (microempresa) puede optar voluntariamente por aplicar el marco del Grupo 2, aplicando los requisitos de la Sección 35 de la NIIF para las Pymes (adopción por primera vez). Grupo 1 vs. Grupo 2 vs. Grupo 3: diferencias clave Aspecto Grupo 1 Grupo 2 Grupo 3 Estándar aplicable NIIF Plenas NIIF para las Pymes Contabilidad simplificada (Decreto 2706 de 2012 y modif.) Tipo de entidad Emisores de valores, entidades de interés público, grandes empresas con vínculos internacionales Pymes medianas y grandes sin interés público Microempresas Activos totales Superiores a 30.000 SMMLV (con condición adicional) Entre 500 y 30.000 SMMLV Hasta 500 SMMLV (excluida vivienda) Empleados Más de 200 (con condición adicional) Entre 11 y 200 Máximo 10 Complejidad de la norma Alta Media Baja Puede migrar voluntariamente a — Grupo 1 Grupo 2 (o Grupo 1) Permanencia y cambio de grupo Un aspecto que suele generar dudas y que la mayoría de contenidos existentes explica de forma incompleta es la regla de permanencia : los preparadores de información financiera que voluntariamente decidan pertenecer al Grupo 2 deben permanecer en él durante un término no inferior a tres (3) años , contados desde su ingreso. Esto aplica tanto si el cambio es voluntario (por ejemplo, una microempresa del Grupo 3 que decide adoptar la NIIF para Pymes) como si es obligatorio por superar los topes establecidos. El proceso de migración, en caso de que se supere el umbral del Grupo 2 y se deba pasar al Grupo 1, sigue normalmente esta secuencia: Año de cumplimiento de requisitos: la entidad detecta que superó los topes y sigue reportando bajo el estándar actual. Año de transición: presenta sus estados financieros bajo el estándar vigente y, adicionalmente, prepara el Estado de Situación Financiera de Apertura (ESFA) bajo el nuevo marco. Año de aplicación plena: presenta sus primeros estados financieros bajo el nuevo marco normativo y debe permanecer allí un mínimo de tres años. Si una entidad quiere cambiar voluntariamente de grupo, debe documentar las razones de la decisión (se trata de un cambio de política contable) e informar al organismo de inspección, vigilancia y control correspondiente, o dejar la evidencia disponible si no está bajo supervisión directa. Cómo implementar la NIIF para las Pymes: guía paso a paso La implementación no es solo un ejercicio contable: involucra a la gerencia, al área financiera, a sistemas y, en muchos casos, a asesores externos. Basado en la experiencia documentada de empresas colombianas que ya pasaron por el proceso, estos son los pasos recomendados: Diagnóstico inicial. Evaluar el sistema contable, administrativo y financiero actual de la empresa, identificar brechas frente a la NIIF para Pymes y detectar las partidas más complejas (inventarios, propiedad planta y equipo, instrumentos financieros, impuesto diferido). Conformación del equipo y capacitación. Definir quién lidera el proceso (contador, gerencia financiera, comité) y capacitar al personal en las secciones relevantes del estándar. La implementación NIIF es responsabilidad de toda la organización, no solo del contador. Diseño de políticas contables. Documentar formalmente los principios, bases y procedimientos que la entidad adoptará para reconocer, medir, presentar y revelar sus estados financieros, conforme a la Sección 10 de la NIIF para Pymes. Elaboración del Estado de Situación Financiera de Apertura (ESFA). Aplicar la Sección 35 (Transición a la NIIF para las Pymes) para reconocer, dar de baja, reclasificar y medir retroactivamente activos, pasivos y patrimonio a la fecha de transición, salvo las exenciones permitidas. Ajustes por transición. Registrar en ganancias acumuladas (o en otra cuenta de patrimonio, si corresponde) los ajustes que surjan de aplicar por primera vez los criterios de reconocimiento y medición de la NIIF para Pymes. Actualización de sistemas y plan de cuentas. Ajustar el software contable y el catálogo de cuentas para que puedan generar información bajo los dos marcos durante el periodo de transición, si aplica. Elaboración de los primeros estados financieros bajo NIIF. Presentar el primer juego completo de estados financieros conforme al nuevo marco, incluyendo la conciliación patrimonial y de resultados frente al marco anterior. Auditoría y verificación interna. Validar que cifras, criterios y reportes estén alineados con la norma; idealmente a cargo de alguien distinto de quien implementó los cambios, para mantener independencia. Actualización continua. La NIIF para Pymes no es estática: cambios en contratos, en el modelo de negocio o enmiendas normativas pueden requerir ajustes posteriores en las políticas contables. Errores comunes al implementar el Grupo 2 Estudios sobre pymes colombianas que atravesaron el proceso de convergencia identifican fallas recurrentes que vale la pena anticipar: No contar con un manual de políticas contables formal , dejando el criterio contable "en la cabeza" del contador en lugar de documentarlo. Sub o sobrevalorar activos totalmente depreciados en el ESFA, olvidando el principio de materialidad: si el valor no es significativo, debe revelarse en notas, no reconocerse como un activo relevante. Ver la capacitación como un gasto y no como una inversión , lo que genera resistencia al cambio y retrasos en el cronograma. Desconocer las sanciones por no implementar oportunamente el marco técnico correspondiente, un vacío común incluso entre responsables contables. Asumir que la implementación es tarea exclusiva del contador , cuando en realidad requiere involucramiento de la gerencia y de las áreas operativas que generan la información financiera. Consecuencias de no aplicar el marco técnico Las entidades obligadas a reportar bajo NIIF que no implementan el marco correspondiente a su grupo se exponen a: Observaciones o sanciones por parte del organismo de inspección, vigilancia y control (Superintendencia de Sociedades, Superintendencia Financiera, Superintendencia de la Economía Solidaria, según el caso). Pérdida de comparabilidad y confiabilidad frente a socios, inversionistas y entidades financieras. Dificultades para acceder a crédito o a procesos de debida diligencia, ya que los estados financieros bajo el marco anterior pueden no ser aceptados por terceros. Novedades recientes que debes tener en cuenta El Decreto 1670 de 2021 modificó los requisitos de permanencia y cambio de grupo, especialmente para el Grupo 3. El Consejo Técnico de la Contaduría Pública (CTCP) ha emitido enmiendas técnicas para el Grupo 2 relacionadas con acuerdos de financiación a proveedores, pasivos no corrientes con condiciones pactadas y la reforma fiscal internacional del "Segundo Pilar" (modificación a la NIC 12), con aplicación proyectada a partir de estados financieros que inicien el 1 de enero de 2026. La futura NIIF 18 (que reemplaza a la NIC 1 en la presentación de estados financieros) entrará en vigor en 2027 para las entidades que apliquen NIIF Plenas; aunque no es de aplicación directa para el Grupo 2, se recomienda que las pymes empiecen a familiarizarse con sus cambios de estructura en el estado de resultados, ya que suele influir en guías posteriores del CTCP. Preguntas frecuentes ¿Una empresa nueva puede pertenecer directamente al Grupo 2? Las entidades recién constituidas se clasifican inicialmente en el Grupo 3 y pueden permanecer allí hasta por tres años, incluso si ya cumplen los requisitos para pertenecer al Grupo 2. Sin embargo, pueden optar voluntariamente por aplicar la NIIF para Pymes desde el inicio si así lo deciden. ¿Qué pasa si mis activos están en un rango pero mis empleados en otro? Cuando exista una combinación de parámetros de planta de personal y activos totales que no coincidan en el mismo grupo, el factor determinante es el valor de los activos totales . ¿Puedo cambiarme voluntariamente del Grupo 2 al Grupo 1? Sí. Las entidades del Grupo 2 pueden aplicar voluntariamente NIIF Plenas, sujetándose a las obligaciones y cronograma correspondientes al Grupo 1. ¿Dónde encuentro el texto oficial y guías prácticas? El Decreto 2420 de 2015 y sus modificatorios están disponibles en el Diario Oficial y en el gestor normativo de la Función Pública. La Superintendencia de Sociedades también publica guías prácticas de aplicación por primera vez y de elaboración del ESFA para orientar a los preparadores de información financiera del Grupo 2.

body_text: Key Takeaways Invoice-to-cash is the path from a finished sale to applied bank funds: invoice out, cash in, reconciled. Three stages carry the load: invoice creation, payment collection, and cash application. Each one is a spot where money moves or stalls. Manual invoice keying still runs at 86% of SMEs, 73% of mid-sized firms, and 35% of enterprises. Every keystroke seeds a downstream error. Around 93% of companies deal with late payments regularly, and that drains working capital right at the collection stage. Nobody agrees on where the cycle even begins. Some vendors scope it narrowly; others treat it as cross-functional. Run invoice-to-cash as one connected flow, not a relay race between disconnected tools, and you get the strongest results. Errors at invoice creation poison everything after. Accurate billing is the foundation, full stop. What “invoice-to-cash” actually means The invoice-to-cash cycle is the sequence that turns a completed sale into money in the bank. It starts when you generate an invoice and ends when the cash lands and gets applied to the right account. Managing it well means looking at the whole journey of a transaction, not treating each step as its own island. Here’s the wrinkle most guides skip. The industry can’t agree on where the cycle begins. Some vendors scope invoice-to-cash narrowly, covering only invoice generation through cash receipt. Others insist it’s a cross-functional workflow spanning sales, operations, finance, and customer teams, one that no single system can own. Both are right, depending on your business model. What are the stages of the invoice-to-cash cycle? Three core stages: invoice creation , payment collection , and cash application . Each is a distinct point where money either moves or gets stuck. Invoice creation. You produce an accurate bill and get it to the customer. When billing details are keyed in by hand, a minor typo turns into a major dispute later, stalling the payment before it ever gets processed. Payment collection. You follow up on what’s owed and chase overdue balances. Delays here hit liquidity directly, and finance teams burn hours sending reminders instead of doing anything strategic. Cash application. You match incoming payments to open invoices. AI-driven matching hits over 90% straight-through processing , so your team stops digging through remittance emails by hand. Why does automation matter here? Automation goes after the two things that kill cash flow: errors and delays. Automated systems can cut Days Sales Outstanding by up to 30% and lift productivity by as much as 70% . One consulting firm squeezed its customer payment cycle from 45 days to 30 just by automating invoicing and reminders. The results scale fast. A multinational manufacturer cut DSO by 25% with automated invoicing and AI collections. Coca-Cola bottlers recovered $33.4 million in deductions, dropping resolution time to 34 days against a 90-day industry average. Here’s the catch. Full automation isn’t always the right call. High-volume repetitive work like cash application and payment reminders warrants complete automation. Judgment-heavy steps like revenue recognition and credit decisions need a human in the loop for audit readiness. Automate the grind, keep eyes on the calls that touch your books. Where SaaS subscription billing breaks the model This is the gap the standard playbook ignores. In SaaS subscription billing, there’s no discrete “order” step. The subscription is the recurring order. When a customer upgrades, downgrades, or renews, that single event is both an order change and a billing change at once. That collapse breaks the tidy invoice-to-cash versus order-to-cash boundary. A proration or renewal doesn’t fit neatly into either bucket. If your billing tool and your collections tool don’t share that context, you’ve built the exact silo the whole cycle is supposed to eliminate. Notice who the case studies feature: Coca-Cola, Konica Minolta, EY, big manufacturers. The automation ROI evidence comes almost entirely from enterprises. Yet the manual-entry burden sits squarely in the SMB and mid-market, exactly where SaaS subscription companies live. The segment with the most to gain gets the least vendor attention. Unifying subscription billing with the rest of invoice-to-cash is how you close that gap. Finding the silos in your financial ops Silos are the invisible walls between the teams and tools that should be moving money together. You see them when sales closes a deal in one system, finance invoices from another, and cash gets applied by hand in a third. You can’t fix what you haven’t named. For SaaS and subscription businesses, the silo problem starts earlier than most guides admit. It starts in the software categories themselves. Any serious invoice-to-cash solution has to reconcile a split the industry baked into its own tooling, and that split is where subscription revenue quietly leaks. What siloed operations look like day to day Silos show up as manual work, blind spots, and slow cash. If your team re-keys the same customer data across billing, collections, and the general ledger, that’s a silo. If nobody can answer “how much will we collect this month?” without a spreadsheet, that’s a silo too. The clearest tell is manual cash application. This is the friction Blixo removes: our matching engine automatically ties payments and balances to invoices from multiple sources with high accuracy, and it gets smarter over time through machine learning. If your team is still matching remittances by hand, you’re carrying a silo automation can lift off your plate. High Days Sales Outstanding is the financial symptom. Cash that should be in your account sits trapped as receivables, and working capital stalls. Delayed payments and reconciliation backlogs are the downstream cost. Why the I2C-vs-O2C boundary is itself a silo Here’s a contradiction worth confronting. When teams strictly separate the invoicing phase from the initial order phase, they build an artificial wall. It forces you to manage customer relationships in fragments, which means misaligned data and slower collections. Both views institutionalize the very silo this article fights: finance on one side, sales and operations on the other. In a recurring revenue model, drawing a hard line between the contract and the bill is impractical. Every mid-cycle adjustment changes the billing schedule, which means the transaction and the invoice are joined at the hip. That’s the case for a unified billing-to-cash platform . When the subscription is the recurring order, splitting order from invoice just rebuilds the wall inside your stack. Blixo runs subscription management, invoicing, collections, and cash application in one place instead of separate tools stitched together. How to spot silos before they cost you cash Start with process mapping . Draw the full path from a signed subscription to applied cash, and mark every point where data gets re-entered or a human waits on another team. Each handoff is a candidate silo. The fixes that work are behavioral, not punitive. Blixo automates collections, chasing, and dunning with your choice of reminders: email, text, phone, letters. Follow-ups happen consistently without manual effort. It also generates and sends invoices from pre-populated items and auto-bills customers using saved payment methods. Put those together and a pattern emerges: most late payment is a communication-and-friction failure, not a solvency problem. For subscription billing, that means dunning workflow design is your highest-use collections investment, not tougher credit terms. Running order-to-cash as one system A unified order-to-cash process runs subscription billing, invoicing, collections, and cash application as one connected system instead of separate tools handing work back and forth. For SaaS businesses this matters a lot. When a customer account changes, the change has to show up instantly across every financial touchpoint, or you get billing discrepancies. Here’s the problem we keep running into. Most invoice-to-cash tooling was built for one-time transactions, so it fumbles the recurring stuff: upgrades, prorations, renewals, usage overages. When your billing engine and your cash application sit in different systems, every plan change becomes a manual reconciliation. Unify them and the recurring order flows into the invoice, then into applied cash. The five pieces that have to connect A unified process connects five things: subscription billing, automated invoice delivery, payment collection, cash application, and dunning. The point is that a subscription event triggers each step without anyone re-keying data. The connective tissue is a shared data model. When all five components read from one customer and contract record, a mid-cycle upgrade updates the billing schedule, regenerates the prorated invoice, and adjusts the next dunning sequence at once. Compare that with stitched-together tools, where a single plan change can spawn three separate tickets across three teams. Two signals tell you the unification is working: the share of invoices generated without manual edits, and the time between a subscription event and its matching journal entry. Both should trend toward near-instant as the seams disappear. Automate everything, or just some steps? Not everything. Automation is great at speed, but certain financial decisions need human oversight. The trick is finding the balance that gives you efficiency without giving up control. Software vendors tend to push complete automation to max out processing speed. Risk people push back, because over-automation invites compliance problems. Routine payment reminders can safely run on software. Evaluating complex credit terms or handling an unusual dispute needs human judgment. Where most implementations get stuck Integration with existing systems is the biggest snag. Bolt an automation layer onto disconnected billing, ERP, and payment tools, and you’ve recreated the silos you were trying to remove. Scope creep is the quieter killer. Teams try to unify all five components at once, the project stalls under its own weight, and it loses executive backing before it proves anything. Roughly two in three finance transformation projects run over their original timeline for exactly this reason. The fix is sequencing, not ambition. Change management is the other blocker. Automation shifts finance work from data entry to exception handling, and teams need training to make that switch. A clean bookings policy is the foundation: get your contract and billing rules right first, then automate on top of them. Start small. Pick one leaky step, unify it end to end, prove the DSO win, then expand. Consolidate onto a single platform and every later automation step draws from the same accurate data source. Measuring ROI and the KPIs that matter You can’t improve what you don’t measure, and for subscription businesses the measurement problem is its own animal. Recurring revenue hides its own leaks. A good financial platform doesn’t just automate the cycle; it reports on it in real time, so you can see whether unifying billing and cash application actually moved the numbers. Start with the right metrics. The whole point of a unified order-to-cash system is turning uncertain receivables into predictable working capital, and a handful of KPIs tell you if it’s working. Which KPIs prove a unified process is working? Track four numbers first: Days Sales Outstanding, payment recovery rate, Collection Effectiveness Index, and bad debt rate. These show how fast cash arrives, how much of it you recover, and how much slips away. For SaaS, add churn-adjusted metrics, since a failed renewal is both a collections miss and a retention miss. DSO is the headline, but track it alongside Best Possible DSO, the figure you’d hit if every customer paid exactly on terms. The gap between the two is your controllable delay, and it’s the number a unified process should shrink quarter over quarter. A CEI above 80 generally signals a healthy collections operation. Below that, cash is leaking somewhere in the handoffs. The revenue upside is smaller but real. Optimizing the cycle end to end tends to add 1-3% to annual revenue, mostly from recovered invoices and fewer write-offs. For a recurring-revenue business, that percentage compounds every billing cycle, so it matters more than the flat number suggests. How to measure ROI on a unified process Compare cost, speed, and recovered cash before and after unification. The clearest wins come from close-cycle time and dispute resolution. One fintech cut its monthly close from six days to four after streamlining order-to-cash. Another useful benchmark: cost per invoice. Manual invoice processing typically runs $15-40 per invoice once labor, errors, and rework are counted; automated processing drops that to a few dollars. Multiply the difference by monthly invoice volume and you’ve got a hard-dollar baseline for ROI. That contrast points to a real market gap. Enterprises have the resources to build custom integrations; smaller growing businesses get stuck with fragmented tools. Put a unified system in early and a mid-market company can scale without adding admin headcount in lockstep with revenue. What makes ROI measurement hard Data quality and integration are the two things that break ROI tracking. If your subscription events live in one system and your cash lands in another, your DSO figure is guesswork. You can’t credit a recovered payment to a process change when the data was never clean to begin with. Where you draw the automation line complicates the math too. Automate too aggressively and the cost of fixing automated errors can wipe out the efficiency gains, which makes the true return hard to isolate. A balanced approach aims automation at predictable, high-volume tasks and keeps complex financial adjustments in manual review. That way the numbers you use to calculate ROI reflect genuine efficiency, not hidden rework. Report on a fixed cadence, monthly at minimum. Review the same KPIs each time so trends surface. A number you check once is a vanity metric. A number you track is a lever. Frequently Asked Questions 1. What’s the difference between invoice-to-cash and order-to-cash? Order-to-cash covers the full sequence from a customer’s initial order through applied payment, including sales and fulfillment. Invoice-to-cash is narrower, starting at invoice generation and ending at cash receipt. In subscription models, these two processes overlap significantly because customer lifecycle events—like plan upgrades or downgrades—instantly trigger both contract updates and new billing calculations. 2. What is dunning, and why does it matter for subscription businesses? Dunning is the structured process of reminding customers about due or overdue payments through scheduled communications. For subscriptions, well-designed dunning workflows recover more revenue than stricter credit terms, since most late payment stems from communication friction, not insolvency. Utilizing multi-channel outreach ensures these reminders reach customers through their preferred contact methods. 3. How is straight-through processing measured in cash application? Straight-through processing measures the percentage of payments automatically matched to open invoices without human intervention. It’s calculated by dividing auto-matched transactions by total incoming payments. Higher rates mean less manual remittance hunting. Modern financial platforms leverage machine learning to continuously refine matching accuracy based on historical payment patterns. 4. What DSO target should a subscription business aim for? A subscription business should aim to minimize the variance between its actual collection times and its optimal terms. This variance highlights operational inefficiencies in billing and collections. Additionally, maintaining a high collection efficiency rate indicates that outstanding balances are being recovered promptly, preserving steady cash flow. 5. How should a small finance team begin automating invoice-to-cash? Begin by identifying the specific touchpoints where billing data is manually transferred between systems. Focus on resolving a single bottleneck first—such as automating payment reminders—to demonstrate immediate value. This phased approach prevents project delays and builds momentum for broader system integration. 6. How do finance roles change after automation is implemented? With automation handling routine tasks, finance professionals transition into analytical roles focused on optimizing cash flow and resolving complex customer accounts. This shift requires training teams to interpret system data and manage exceptions. To ensure a smooth transition, establish clear operational guidelines before deploying new software. 7. What makes a unified platform better than integrating separate billing and collections tools? A unified platform operates on a single database, ensuring that any change to a customer’s subscription status instantly updates their billing schedule and collection path. This eliminates the data discrepancies that occur when separate systems attempt to sync. By consolidating these functions, businesses reduce administrative overhead and eliminate the need to maintain complex API integrations.

title: Alvotech further strengthens liquidity by securing term loan facility of $75 million
summary: $75 million additional term loan facility maturing December 31, 2027, led by GoldenTree Asset Management Follows recent $165m equity raise strengthening cash position Including equity financing and undrawn loan facility, Alvotech has secured access to $240 million in new capital Funds will support
body_text: $75 million additional term loan facility maturing December 31, 2027, led by GoldenTree Asset Management Follows recent $165m equity raise strengthening cash position Including equity financing and undrawn loan facility, Alvotech has secured access to $240 million in new capital Funds will support execution across Alvotech’s R&D pipeline and global product launches REYKJAVIK, ICELAND (July 1, 2026) — Alvotech (NASDAQ: ALVO; ALVO-SDB), a global biotechnology company specializing in the development and manufacture of biosimilar medicines for patients worldwide, today announced that it has amended its existing credit agreement with funds managed by GoldenTree Asset Management LP and other existing lenders of Alvotech to provide a term loan facility of up to $75 million in additional capital. The financing further strengthens Alvotech's financial position following the $165 million equity capital raise announced on June 18, 2026, and supports the continued execution of the company's growth strategy, including advancing its biosimilar pipeline, supporting product launches and expanding global commercial operations. Including the equity financing and the undrawn term loan facility the company has secured access to $240 million in new capital. “This financing provides additional flexibility as we continue to execute on our strategic priorities and support the next phase of growth for Alvotech," said Robert Wessman, founder and chairman of Alvotech. “The strong support we received from both existing shareholders and more than 40 new specialist healthcare investors in our recent equity offering, together with this additional financing, reflects growing confidence in Alvotech, our strategy and the opportunities ahead. “Over the past several months we have achieved important milestones across our business, including the resubmission of key Biologics License Applications to the FDA, continued advancement of our pipeline including FDA acceptance of our BLA for a biosimilar to Entyvio®, and the expansion of our global commercial footprint. These achievements reinforce our belief that we are building one of the world’s leading biosimilars companies. “With approximately 30 biosimilar products in development and a growing portfolio of commercial opportunities, we see a significant opportunity to increase patient access to affordable biologic medicines around the world. “Capital is the fuel that enables us to execute on that vision, and this financing further strengthens our ability to invest in growth and create long-term value for patients, partners and shareholders.” The financing builds on Alvotech's existing relationship with GoldenTree, which has been a long-term financing partner to the company. It expands the company’s existing credit agreement by providing an additional $75 million term loan facility alongside the $100 million term loan facility announced in December 2025. It bears an interest rate of 12.50%, payable monthly in cash, and has a maturity date of December 31, 2027. For further information, contact: Media Benedikt Stefansson Sarah MacLeod alvotech.media@alvotech.com Investors Dr. Balaji V Prasad Benedikt Stefansson alvotech.ir@alvotech.com About Alvotech Alvotech is a biotechnology company, founded by Robert Wessman, focused solely on the development and manufacture of biosimilar medicines for patients worldwide. Alvotech seeks to be a global leader in biosimilars by delivering high-quality, cost-effective products and services, enabled by a fully integrated approach and broad in-house capabilities. Five biosimilars are already approved and marketed in multiple global markets, including biosimilars to Humira® (adalimumab), Stelara® (ustekinumab), Simponi® (golimumab), Eylea® (aflibercept) and Prolia®/Xgeva® (denosumab). The current development pipeline includes nine disclosed biosimilar candidates aimed at treating autoimmune disorders, eye disorders, osteoporosis, respiratory disease, and cancer. Alvotech has formed a network of strategic commercial partnerships to provide global reach and leverage local expertise in markets that include the United States, Europe, Japan, China, and other Asian countries and large parts of South America, Africa and the Middle East. For more information, please visit https://www.alvotech.com . None of the information on the Alvotech website shall be deemed part of this press release.
